meta.description: Help your child separate their decisions from others' emotions and stop saying yes just because "saying no feels awkward." Course for kids 8–12.

hero.headline: Does your child say "yes" just to keep others from being upset?
hero.subheadline: "You'll upset me," "I'll be offended," "that would hurt my feelings." Your child hears this — and picks someone else's mood over their own "no."

media.alt: A child agrees to avoid hurting an adult's feelings

pain.title: Emotional blackmail: when "no" feels scarier than "yes"
pain.body:
"You'll upset me." "That would hurt." "I'll be offended." It happens at school, from a friend, a relative, a classmate. Instead of a request, your child hears a warning: if you say no, this person will feel bad — and it'll be your fault.

This isn't a request — it's emotional blackmail. The adult (or peer) doesn't explain why it matters, doesn't propose to talk it through. They simply transfer responsibility for their own mood onto your child: "you decide whether I'll be okay." To avoid the preemptive guilt, the child agrees. They do what's "right" — not what they want.

Without the skill to recognize this technique, your child picks the option that "keeps the peace" every time. Their own "wants" go quiet. By age 10–11, they may not know what they want — because they've learned to ask "how will the other person feel if I say no?" first.
